results.title: Avoid Local Minima and Saddle Points in Numerical Optimization
results.content: # How do you avoid local minima and saddle points in numerical optimization? Numerical optimization is the process of finding the optimal values of a function or a system of equations using numerical methods. However, numerical optimization can be challenging when the function or system has multiple local minima or saddle points, which are points where the gradient is zero but the function value is not optimal. In this article, you will learn some strategies to avoid getting stuck in these points and improve your numerical optimization results. Gradient descent is a popular numerical optimization method that iteratively updates the values of the variables by moving in the direction of the steepest descent of the function. Stochastic methods are numerical optimization methods that introduce some randomness or noise in the search process. Stochastic methods can help avoid local minima and saddle points by escaping from them with some probability, depending on the temperature or noise level. Global methods are numerical optimization methods that aim to find the global minimum of the function, rather than a local one. Global methods can help avoid local minima and saddle points by maintaining a diversity of solutions and applying crossover and mutation operators that create new solutions from existing ones. Convex optimization is a special case of numerical optimization where the function or system is convex, meaning that it has a single global minimum and no local minima or saddle points. Convex optimization can be solved efficiently and reliably using various numerical methods, such as gradient descent, interior point methods, or simplex methods. Convex optimization can help avoid local minima and saddle points by transforming the original problem into a convex one, if possible, or by using convex relaxation or approximation techniques that replace the original problem with a convex one that is easier to solve. Multimodal optimization can help avoid local minima and saddle points by using methods that can detect and explore different modes or regions of the function, such as clustering, niching, or multi-objective optimization methods. I'm learning convex optimization and have just learnt about the concave-convex procedure (CCCP) for minimizing objective functions that can be written as a convex function plus a concave function. I studied an example and found that CCCP can descend into a local minimum. $$\mbox{Minimize }\,f(x) = ax-bx^2+cx^4,$$. where $\,a=0.5,\,b=2,\,c=0.25\,$ are all positive. The convex part is $\,ax+cx^4$ and the concave part is $-bx^2$. CCCP finds the minimum iteratively starting from an initial guess $\,x\_0$. To obtain $\,x\_{n+1}\,$ from $\,x\_n$, the concave part is linearized around $\,x\_n\,$ to obtain. $$f\_{x\_n}(x)=ax+cx^4-bx\_n^2-2bx\_n(x-x\_n).$$. One then minimizes the convex function $f\_{x\_n}(x)$ to find. $$x\_{n+1}=\left(\frac{2bx\_n-a}{4c}\right)^{1/3}.$$. The iteration descends into the global minimum at $x=-2.05979\,$ if $\,x\_0<x\_c=0.125494$, and descends into the local minimum at $x=1.934298\,$ if $\,x\_0>x\_c$. Also, the convergence rate of CCCP is first-order (exponential), slower than Newton's method which has second-order convergence. Am I understanding CCCP correctly? In what sense is difference-of-convex (DC) programming easier to solve, then, compared with a general non-convex optimization problem? I am trying to solve an optimisation problem consisting in finding the global maximum of a high dimensional (10+) monotonic function (as in monotonic in every direction). I have coded the whole thing in `pyomo` and I am using the `ipopt` solver. In most cases, I am confident it converges successfully to the global optimal. But if I play a bit with the constraints I see that it sometimes converges to a local minima. I have looked into the options that can be passed to `ipopt` and the list is so long that I cannot understand which parameters to play with to help with the convergence to the global minima. my variables used to be defined with very infinite bounds, e.g. `bounds=(0,None)` to move on the infinite half-line. I have enforced two finite bounds on them. I am now using multiple starts with:. results = opt.solve(self.model, solver='ipopt', strategy='midpoint_guess_and_bound')`. So far this has made my happy with the convergence. Learning is a mess's user avatar. ## 1 Answer 1. Sorry, IPOPT is a local solver. If you really want to find global solutions, you can use a global solver such as Baron, Couenne or Antigone. There is a trade-off: global solvers are slower and may not work for large problems. Alternatively, you can help local solvers with a good initial point. Sometimes multistart algorithms are used to prevent bad local optima: use a bunch of different starting points.
